questions.q: After ATP has its terminal phosphate removed, what is left behind in the cell?
questions.why: ATP is 'spent' by cutting off the terminal phosphate; what stays in the cell is ADP, and putting the phosphate back on recharges it.

questions.q: In a molecular cloning experiment, the ampicillin resistance marker on the plasmid, used to select bacteria that have successfully taken up the plasmid, is called what?
questions.why: Amp is the ampicillin resistance marker on the plasmid; only bacteria that have taken up the plasmid and express the resistance can grow on ampicillin-containing plates. It is a different term from AMP (adenosine monophosphate).

questions.q: On the chain ATP → ADP → AMP, where the number of phosphates falls step by step, what is left after ATP has used up two phosphates?
questions.why: ATP → ADP → AMP is a chain with a decreasing number of phosphates; a high AMP concentration usually means the cell is short of energy, so AMPK is switched on, shutting down ATP-consuming processes and opening up ATP-producing ones.

questions.q: The building half of metabolism: spends energy to assemble small molecules into proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. What is this half called?
questions.why: Metabolism has two halves: catabolism breaks things down and harvests energy; anabolism builds them and costs ATP, which is why cancer cells depend on anabolism so heavily.

questions.q: Which amino acid, left sitting in a protein for a long time, is the one most prone to deamidation?
questions.why: The amide next to asparagine spontaneously loses an ammonia molecule to become succinimide, then takes up water to become aspartic acid or iso-aspartic acid; this is a common reason for therapeutic proteins to go wrong within their shelf life.

questions.q: The acidic amino acid produced when asparagine is deamidated and then takes up water, the one that is not the stereoisomer (its side chain ends in a carboxyl group), is called what?
questions.why: Aspartic acid is the normal product of asparagine deamidation (115.03 Da); iso-aspartic acid has the same mass but a different stereochemistry, so therapeutic proteins need chromatography to separate the two.

questions.q: The smallest unit of an element; a molecule is built by binding atoms together. What is this unit called?
questions.why: The atom is the smallest unit of an element, while a molecule is the result of atoms bonding covalently; carbon, because it is tetravalent and can form many bonds, becomes the backbone of organic chemistry.

questions.q: The dense centre of an atom, which houses protons and neutrons. Where is almost all of an atom's mass concentrated?
questions.why: Almost all of an atom's mass sits in the tiny-diameter atomic nucleus, while the electron cloud occupies nearly all the volume yet almost no mass; the number of protons in the nucleus is the element's atomic number.

questions.q: The cell's only universal energy currency, the molecule made of adenine, ribose and three phosphates, is called what?
questions.why: ATP is made of adenine, ribose and three phosphates; what the cell actually spends is the bond between the terminal phosphate and the one next to it, and removing the terminal phosphate leaves ADP.

questions.q: One of the four letters of DNA (A, T, G, C), with U replacing T in RNA. What is this class of molecule called?
questions.why: The four bases differ only in their side functional group, and that difference sets the pairing rules: G–C makes three hydrogen bonds and A–T makes two, so the higher the GC content, the higher the Tm.

questions.q: Molecules made by living systems: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. What is the collective name for these four classes?
questions.why: The first lecture splits biomolecules into four classes and gives them four roles: biomarker, energy source, structure and signal; it is the action of these molecules that links genotype to phenotype.

questions.q: One of the four major biomolecules; mainly a fuel, but also a structural material like cellulose. What is this class called?
questions.why: Carbohydrates are divided by complexity into monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides; glycogen and starch are for storage, cellulose is for structure, and the liver and kidneys release free glucose through glucose-6-phosphatase.

questions.q: Four electrons in its outermost shell, able to form covalent bonds with four atoms, so it can chain into long chains, rings and double bonds. Which element is the centre of the organic chemistry of life?
questions.why: Carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell, so it can build long carbon chains, ring structures and double bonds, and the backbones of sugars, lipids, amino acids and nucleotides are all centred on carbon.

questions.q: The breakdown half of metabolism: taking large molecules apart and releasing energy. What is this half called?
questions.why: Metabolism has two halves: catabolism breaks large molecules down to harvest energy, anabolism spends energy to build; his cancer metabolism example is built exactly on this division of labour.

questions.q: Its glycosidic bonds run in the opposite direction to those of starch, forming straight parallel fibres, which is why the bacteria in a cow's stomach can cut these bonds and you cannot. This structural polysaccharide is called ______.
questions.why: Cellulose is the structural form in plants, held together by glycosidic bonds running in the opposite direction to those of starch to form parallel fibres; because humans have no enzyme that cuts these bonds, cellulose can only pass through as faeces.

questions.q: The hamster cell line used to manufacture human therapeutic proteins, adopted because it attaches the correct sugars. What is it called?
questions.why: When you move a gene into a CHO cell for expression you have to do codon optimisation; because CHO cells add the sugars, the glycosylation of the therapeutic protein comes out correct.

questions.q: The lipid embedded in membranes that keeps them fluid even at low temperature. What is it called?
questions.why: Cholesterol sits within the bilayer to modulate its fluidity; blood is water-based and lipids cannot get through it, so they are packaged into lipoproteins for transport.

questions.q: Rewriting a gene into the codon spelling the host cell prefers, so that the protein is easy to make. What is this called?
questions.why: Different species prefer different codons for the same amino acid, so when you move a gene into a CHO cell for expression you have to do codon optimisation, otherwise the protein is hard to make.

questions.q: The same amino acid is written with different codons that different species prefer. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.why: Codon usage is the preference for codons between species; codon-usage bias is the skew that this preference produces, and it has to be readjusted when a gene moves between species.

questions.q: Why does the codon spelling have to be readjusted when a gene is moved from one species into a CHO cell for expression?
options: Each species uses a different sugar in its DNA and RNA
Different species prefer different codons for the same amino acid, so once the gene is moved across, the preference no longer matches
The start and stop codons are completely different in different species
The length of an amino acid's side chain determines the length of its codon
questions.why: Codon-usage bias is precisely about the differences in codon preference between species; that is why codon optimisation rewrites the gene into the spelling the host prefers.

questions.q: A chemical substance formed by combining two or more elements. What is it called?
questions.why: This site defines a compound as a chemical substance formed by combining two or more elements; a molecule is two or more atoms joined together in a fixed way.

questions.q: Healthy cells stop dividing as soon as they touch a neighbour. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.why: Healthy cells stop dividing as soon as they touch a neighbour; the Hippo pathway uses exactly this cell contact to switch growth off — MST1 activates LATS1, LATS1 phosphorylates YAP, and YAP is held outside the nucleus.

questions.q: Atoms are held together by three kinds of attraction: the kind in which two atoms share a pair of electrons and pull each other together is called ______.
questions.why: A covalent bond is two atoms sharing a pair of electrons, and it forms the backbone of most biomolecules; the other two are the electrostatic attraction of the ionic bond and the sideways attraction of the hydrogen bond.

questions.q: After the phospholipid signalling pathway PI → PI(4)P → PI(4,5)P is cleaved, what is the second messenger that stays on the cell membrane called?
questions.why: The lecturer's Slide 19 pathway is PI → PI(4)P → PI(4,5)P → DAG + IP3, with DAG staying on the membrane as the second messenger.

questions.q: The movement in which molecules spread spontaneously from where there are many to where there are few, at no energy cost. What is it called?
questions.why: Diffusion costs no energy; molecules move down the concentration gradient from more to fewer, making it the simplest way of transporting substances.

questions.q: The class of carbohydrate in which two sugar units are joined together, such as sucrose. What is it called?
questions.why: Carbohydrates are divided by complexity into monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides; a disaccharide is two sugar units joined together, and the bond that links the units is called a glycosidic bond.

questions.q: The molecule written with the four letters A, T, G and C, kept in the nucleus as the master instruction manual. What is it called?
questions.why: DNA is that master instruction manual; RNA is the family that reads and executes the instructions in DNA, while nucleic acid is the whole class of molecules that includes DNA and RNA.

questions.q: The particle that carries a negative charge, moves around the atomic nucleus and does all the bonding. What is it called?
questions.why: Outside the nucleus are the negatively charged electrons, arranged in layers on electron shells; a covalent bond is simply two atoms sharing a pair of electrons.

questions.q: The fixed energy layer outside the atomic nucleus; the outermost one determines what an atom can bond with. This layer is called ______.
questions.why: An electron shell is the fixed energy layer outside the atomic nucleus, and the outermost shell decides what an atom can bond with; carbon can take on four 'hands' precisely because its outermost shell is never full.

questions.q: The toxic part of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria is in fact which of the following molecules?
questions.why: Endotoxin and LPS are the same molecule; once LPS is recognised by TLR4 it switches on the IKK, IκB and NF-κB cascade, and too much of it causes septic shock.

questions.q: The capacity to do work; in the cell it comes from the net release of metabolic reactions. What is this concept called?
questions.why: In the cell, energy is not warmth but the capacity to do work; it comes from the breaking of chemical bonds and is captured as ATP.

questions.q: A string of carbons with a small acidic end; whether the chain has a double bond decides whether it is saturated or unsaturated. What is this class of molecule called?
questions.why: A fatty acid is the building unit of lipids; one with a double bond in the chain is an unsaturated fatty acid, whose chain kinks, packs loosely and is an oil at room temperature.

questions.q: The long carbon tail of a fatty acid, which is itself saturated or unsaturated. What is this tail called?
questions.why: A fatty-acid chain is that long carbon tail of a fatty acid; whether the tail carries a double bond is what decides whether the whole thing is saturated or unsaturated.

questions.q: The small group of atoms on a molecule that gives it its chemical character and reactivity — hydroxyl, carboxyl, amino and phosphate groups are all of this kind. It is called ______.
questions.why: The carbon chain is only the handle; what really decides a molecule's temperament is the functional group on that chain; he says explicitly that the structures of functional groups are not examined, but the phosphate group is worth remembering.

questions.q: The monosaccharide that cells burn as fuel. What is it called?
questions.why: Glucose is the energy currency of the cell; the liver and kidneys use glucose-6-phosphatase to release it in free form, and lacking that enzyme produces glycogen storage disease.

questions.q: The same chain of glucose does a completely different job depending on its shape: the storage form of animals and fungi, whose branching lets the cell release sugar rapidly from several positions at once, is ______.
questions.why: Glycogen is the storage form of glucose in animals and fungi, with α1,4 linkages and α1,6 branch points; the storage form in plants is starch.

questions.q: The chemical link between one sugar unit and the next in a sugar chain. What is it called?
questions.why: Glycosidic bonds join sugar units into disaccharides and polysaccharides; the glycosidic bonds of starch and cellulose run in opposite directions, which is why one can store and the other can resist tension.

questions.q: Water has four jobs in the cell, and one of them is this — the energy needed to raise the temperature of a substance by one degree — which keeps body temperature from swinging wildly as the cell works.
questions.why: Water's high specific heat keeps body temperature stable; its high melting point also comes from the hydrogen-bond network — the hydrogen bonds have to be broken before it can melt.

questions.q: When the Hippo pathway is switched off, MST1 activates LATS1 and LATS1 phosphorylates YAP. What is the result?
options: The cell switches to aerobic glycolysis, fermenting glucose into lactate
YAP enters the nucleus, binds TEAD and drives tissue overgrowth
The cell is recognised by TLR4, which starts the NF-κB inflammation cascade
Phosphorylated YAP is kept in the cytoplasm and degraded, and the cell stops proliferating
questions.why: Phosphorylated YAP is held in the cytoplasm by 14-3-3 and degraded, so the cell no longer divides; when the pathway fails, YAP enters the nucleus and binds TEAD, and only then does overgrowth occur.

questions.q: Atoms are held together by three kinds of attraction: the covalent bond, the ionic bond, and the one between a slightly positive hydrogen and a nearby slightly negative oxygen or nitrogen. That last one is the ______.
questions.why: Hydrogen bonds are the weakest, yet they can break and reform at any time — which is exactly why proteins can fold and DNA can unwind; three hydrogen bonds for G–C and two for A–T are the precise numbers he listed.

questions.q: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, the kind of bond you see in table salt. It is called ______.
questions.why: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; together with the covalent bond and the hydrogen bond it makes up the three attractions that hold atoms together.

questions.q: iso-aspartic acid has the same mass as true aspartic acid (115.03 Da) but a different stereochemistry. What is the consequence of that difference?
options: It affects protein folding and binding capacity differently from true aspartic acid
It has no effect at all, because the mass is the same
It only changes the charge of the protein and does not affect its shape
It makes the protein fold back automatically into the same shape, with its function unchanged
questions.why: The two differ in how they are bonded, so they also differ in their effect on protein folding and binding capacity; manufacturers of therapeutic proteins have to use chromatography to separate iso-Asp from genuine Asp.

questions.q: In the inflammation cascade LPS → TLR4 → IKK → IκB → NF-κB, what is IKK's job?
options: To remove the phosphate from IκB and restore its activity
To keep NF-κB outside the nucleus
To add a phosphate onto IκB, which is the mark that it is to be destroyed
questions.why: IκB kinase (IKK) puts a phosphate onto IκB, marking it for destruction; once IκB has been destroyed, NF-κB can enter the nucleus and switch on inflammatory genes.

questions.q: The enzyme that adds a phosphate group to another protein, usually switching it on. What is this enzyme called?
questions.why: A kinase takes the terminal phosphate off ATP and sticks it onto a protein, and the negatively charged phosphate pushes the protein apart; a phosphatase uses water to remove the phosphate and switches the toggle back.

questions.q: The family of molecules that fear water: building walls, storing energy and also carrying signals. What is this family called?
questions.why: Lipids are insoluble in water: phospholipids are the backbone of membranes, triglycerides are fuel stores, and LPS is the source of the inflammatory signal.

questions.q: The sheet-like structure two molecules thick that forms the cell membrane, with heads facing out and tails facing in. What is it called?
questions.why: Phospholipids are amphipathic, with hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails, so in water they arrange themselves into a bilayer with no energy at all; cholesterol is embedded in the middle to regulate fluidity.

questions.q: The particle wrapped in protein that carries lipids around the blood. What is it called?
questions.why: Blood is water-based and lipids cannot get through it, so they are packaged into lipoproteins for transport.

questions.q: When the LPS of the Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane is in excess, what does it ultimately cause?
options: Contact inhibition, so cells stop dividing
The Warburg effect, with cancer cells switching to aerobic glycolysis
Glycogen storage disease, in which liver cells cannot release free glucose
questions.why: Once LPS is recognised by TLR4 it switches on the IKK, IκB and NF-κB cascade to trigger inflammation; too much of it causes septic shock, which he says is a common cause of death among surgical intensive-care patients.

questions.q: A very large molecule, such as a protein or a nucleic acid, built from many small units. What is this called?
questions.why: A macromolecule is a large molecule built from many small units: proteins are strings of amino acids, nucleic acids are strings of nucleotides.

questions.q: Metabolism has two halves: catabolism breaks large molecules down and harvests the energy, anabolism builds them and spends energy to assemble large molecules. The two together are called ______.
questions.why: Metabolism is the collective name for all the chemical reactions of the cell; his cancer metabolism example is built exactly on this division of labour between breaking down and building up.

questions.q: The study of life at the molecular level, especially DNA, RNA and proteins. What is this field called?
questions.why: Molecular biology studies life at the molecular level; what it deals with is precisely the two classes of biomolecules, nucleic acids and proteins.

questions.q: The product of two or more atoms joined together in a fixed way, and therefore having a shape and its own properties. What is it called?
questions.why: A molecule is the product of atoms joining in a fixed way; and molecules have shapes, and the shape decides what a molecule can encounter.

questions.q: A single sugar unit, such as glucose or fructose. What is this class of carbohydrate called?
questions.why: Carbohydrates are divided by complexity into monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides; a monosaccharide is the smallest sugar unit.

questions.q: The particle that carries no charge, sits in the atomic nucleus and only adds mass without changing chemical properties. What is it called?
questions.why: A neutron adds mass but does not change chemical properties; one more or one fewer neutron makes a different isotope, which is why carbon-14 can be used for dating.

questions.q: The four great families in the first lecture are biomolecules: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and the ______ to which DNA and RNA belong.
questions.why: Nucleic acids are the family that carries information: DNA is the instruction manual, RNA is the photocopy that reads and executes the manual.

questions.q: Nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate; take the phosphate away and only base + sugar is left. This building block before the phosphate is added is called ______.
questions.why: The first lecture defines it explicitly: nucleoside = base + sugar; and the building unit of DNA and RNA is the nucleotide, base + sugar + phosphate.

questions.q: The building unit of DNA and RNA is base + sugar + phosphate. What is this three-part package called?
questions.why: On the central dogma diagram, 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons correspond to 20 amino acids; ATP is itself a nucleotide, and DNA and ATP use the same part.

questions.q: The process of losing electrons (or gaining oxygen), which releases energy. What is it called?
questions.why: Oxidation is losing electrons and reduction is gaining them, and the two always happen together; when the cell burns sugar the sugar is oxidised and the oxygen is reduced, and the released energy is captured as ATP.

questions.q: pH changes the charge of a molecule, the charge changes the shape, and the shape changes the function; the therapeutic protein deamidation example from his first lecture happens in a ______ environment.
questions.why: pH is an acid–base scale: 7 is neutral, below that is acidic and above it is alkaline, and each step is a factor of ten; at high pH asparagine is deamidated to succinimide, with the mass going 114.04 → 97.02 → 115.03 Da.

questions.q: The enzyme that uses water to remove the phosphate group and switches the protein back off. What is it called?
questions.why: A kinase uses ATP to add a phosphate and switch the protein on, a phosphatase uses water to remove the phosphate and switch it off — on and off is the cell's fastest toggle.

questions.q: The molecule with one hydrophilic end and one hydrophobic end, which is precisely why membranes can assemble themselves. What is it called?
questions.why: Phospholipids are amphipathic: hydrophilic head, hydrophobic tail, so in water they arrange themselves into a bilayer with no energy required.

questions.q: The phosphorylation switch: a kinase takes the terminal phosphate off ATP and sticks it onto a protein. This step is called ______.
questions.why: Attaching a phosphate group is usually what switches a protein on; his entire Hippo–YAP example runs on this mechanism.

questions.q: A molecule with a slight positive charge at one end and a slight negative charge at the other, like a small magnet. What is this property called?
questions.why: Like attracts like, which is why water dissolves salts and sugars but rejects oil; the water molecule is bent because oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer, and that is what gives it polarity.

questions.q: Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen: a single sugar unit is a monosaccharide, two joined together are a disaccharide, and a long chain is a ______, with the units linked by glycosidic bonds.
questions.why: A long chain of sugar units is a polysaccharide, such as glycogen, starch or cellulose; the same chain of glucose does a completely different job depending on its shape.

questions.q: The machine folded from a string of amino acid beads, whose shape decides what it does. What is this class of molecule called?
questions.why: A protein is a machine that has been folded, and shape decides function; enzymes, receptors, antibodies and the cytoskeleton are all proteins.

questions.q: For an enzyme that attaches a phosphate group to another protein (ATP is its fuel), what is its typical role in the cell?
options: Switching a protein on, for instance keeping YAP out of the nucleus as in the Hippo pathway
Switching a protein off by removing the phosphate
Cutting the protein into short fragments
Delivering the protein into the nucleus
questions.why: ATP supplies the phosphate, the kinase adds it and the phosphatase removes it with water; his entire Hippo example runs on this phosphorylation switch.

questions.q: The positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus whose number determines the identity of the element. What is it called?
questions.why: The number of protons determines which element it is (hydrogen 1, carbon 6, oxygen 8), and the number of neutrons determines which isotope it is.

questions.q: Which of the following does 'Pyrogen' mean?
options: The collapse that follows sepsis overwhelming the body's own inflammatory response.
A substance that raises body temperature and causes fever.
The liquid into which other things dissolve; for the cell that liquid is water.
A particle wrapped in protein that carries lipids around the blood.
questions.why: A pyrogen is a substance that raises body temperature and causes fever; septic shock, by contrast, is the collapse that follows the body's own inflammatory response being overwhelmed.

questions.q: Why do cancer cells send most of their pyruvate to become lactate even when oxygen is available?
options: Because glycolysis cannot take place at all in cancer cells
Because the mitochondria of cancer cells have already disappeared
Because what it wants are the raw materials (nucleotides, lipids, amino acids), not fuel
Because oxygen is toxic to cancer cells
questions.why: Half-broken-down sugar molecules are ideal building material for nucleotides, lipids and amino acids; a cell that has to divide a billion times is far short of building material rather than of fuel.

questions.q: The process of gaining electrons (or losing oxygen), which stores energy in a molecule. What is it called?
questions.why: Oxidation and reduction always happen together; when the cell burns sugar the sugar is oxidised and the oxygen is reduced, and the released energy is captured as ATP.

questions.q: A whole family of molecules that reads and executes the instructions in DNA. What is it called?
questions.why: RNA is the family that reads and executes the instructions in DNA, and both DNA and RNA belong to the nucleic acids; the sugar in RNA is ribose, while the sugar in DNA is deoxyribose.

questions.q: The collapse that follows sepsis overwhelming the body's own inflammatory response is caused by over-activation of which cascade?
options: The LPS → TLR4 → IKK → IκB → NF-κB inflammation cascade
The repair pathway that follows DNA damage
questions.why: LPS is recognised by TLR4 and the cascade switches on NF-κB through IKK and IκB; too much of it causes septic shock.

questions.q: Water has four jobs in the cell: it is the ______, it is a participant in the reactions of proteins and ATP, it holds macromolecules in three-dimensional shape through hydrogen bonds, and its high specific heat keeps body temperature stable.
questions.why: Water is the solvent of the cell and also a participant in the chemistry of proteins and ATP; its polarity makes it both the best solvent and the most stable environment.

questions.q: The polysaccharide plants use to store sugar, the storage form of glucose. What is it called?
questions.why: Starch is the storage form in plants, glycogen is the storage form in animals and fungi, and cellulose is the structural form.

questions.q: AUG, the signal to start translation, which also codes for methionine. What is this codon called?
questions.why: On the central dogma diagram the start codon is AUG and the stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA.

questions.q: UAA, UAG, UGA — translation stops here. What is this kind of codon called?
questions.why: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons correspond to 20 amino acids; the start is AUG and the stops are UAA, UAG and UGA.

questions.q: At high pH asparagine is deamidated, becoming a ______ intermediate, then taking up water to become aspartate or isoaspartate, with the mass going from 114.04 Da to 97.02 Da.
questions.why: Succinimide is the short-lived intermediate formed when asparagine is deamidated; because deamidation is a function of time, the storage conditions and shelf life of therapeutic proteins are strictly regulated.

questions.q: Which of the following does 'Sugar (carbohydrate)' mean?
options: One of the four major biomolecules; mainly a fuel, and also a building material.
The monosaccharide that cells burn as fuel.
The family of molecules that fear water: building walls, storing energy and also carrying signals.
The class of biomolecules that includes DNA and RNA. It carries information.
questions.why: The entry Sugar (carbohydrate) is exactly the carbohydrate class: one of the four major biomolecules, mainly a fuel and also a building material (carbohydrates are also structural materials such as cellulose).

questions.q: The backbone of one DNA strand is built from alternating sugar and phosphate groups; the phosphate group actually has two jobs. What is the second one?
options: It is the source of the hydrogen bonds that set the stability of the double helix
It holds DNA and RNA together on the same molecule
It is the signal tag used when mRNA is spliced
It is ATP's energy wallet, so ATP is itself a kind of nucleotide
questions.why: The phosphate group props up the backbone and is also ATP's energy wallet; ATP is therefore itself a nucleotide, and DNA and ATP use the same part.

questions.q: In the inflammation cascade LPS → TLR4 → IKK → IκB → NF-κB, what is TLR4's role?
options: Adding a phosphate to IκB and marking it for destruction
The cell-surface receptor that recognises LPS, the first stop in the cascade
Delivering NF-κB into the nucleus to switch on genes
Cutting the bacterium open and releasing the LPS
questions.why: Once TLR4 recognises LPS it switches on the IKK, IκB and NF-κB cascade, which is precisely the cascade stem he set out in the first lecture.

questions.q: Three fatty acids attached to one glycerol, the way the body stores fuel. What is this called?
questions.why: A triglyceride is the body's fuel store; blood is water-based, so lipids have to be packaged into lipoproteins for transport.

questions.q: A fatty acid with one or more double bonds in its chain, which therefore bends and cannot pack tightly. What is it called?
questions.why: A fatty acid with a double bond in the chain is an unsaturated fatty acid: the chain kinks, packs loosely and is an oil at room temperature; a saturated fatty acid without double bonds is straight and packs tightly.

questions.q: The water molecule is bent, with a partial positive charge at one end and a partial negative charge at the other; this shape gives four biological reasons. Which one is it?
options: It lines amino acids up into the base sequence of DNA
It cleaves off the terminal phosphate of ATP to release energy
It turns proteins into properly folded enzymes
It is the solvent in which every reaction takes place, and the source of the three-dimensional shape of macromolecules
questions.why: The four reasons for water are: it is the solvent, it participates in the chemistry of proteins and ATP, it gives macromolecules their three-dimensional shape through hydrogen bonds, and its high specific heat keeps body temperature stable.
